security_leads.technique_name: TCP MD5 Absence / Lack of Transport Authentication
security_leads.description: Step 1: BGP relies on TCP for transport but the base protocol (RFC 4271) does not mandate authentication for the TCP connection itself. Step 2: An attacker on-path or able to spoof IP addresses can initiate a TCP connection to port 179. Step 3: Without TCP MD5 (RFC 2385) or other transport-layer authentication enabled, the attacker can complete the TCP handshake and proceed to exchange BGP OPEN messages, effectively bypassing any implicit authentication and establishing a rogue BGP session to inject or hijack routes.

rfc_references.quote: Absent the use of mechanisms that effect these security services, attackers can disrupt these TCP connections and/or masquerade as a legitimate peer router.
Implementations MUST support TCP MD5 [RFC2385] for authentication.

prerequisites: Attacker can reach the BGP speaker's IP/port 179
TCP MD5 authentication is not configured or supported on the target
security_leads.mitigation: Mandatory deployment of TCP MD5 (RFC 2385) or stronger transport security mechanisms (e.g., IPsec, TLS over BGP) to authenticate the TCP connection before BGP session establishment.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP Message Header Length Field Manipulation
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker crafts a BGP message with a valid header but sets the Length field to a value larger than the maximum allowed message size (4096 octets) or larger than the actual payload. Step 2: The victim BGP speaker parses the Length field and attempts to read the entire message based on this length. Step 3: If the implementation does not validate that the length field does not exceed the maximum allowed size or the actual received data, it may read out-of-bounds memory, causing a crash or information leak. Step 4: If the implementation allocates memory based on the length field without checking against system limits, it could lead to resource exhaustion.

rfc_references.quote: Length: This 2-octet unsigned integer indicates the total length of the message, including the header in octets. ... The value of the Length field MUST always be at least 19 and no greater than 4096
if the Length field of the message header is less than 19 or greater than 4096, ... then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Bad Message Length.

prerequisites: Attacker can send BGP messages to the victim
Victim implementation fails to validate Length field against maximum size (4096 octets)
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of the Length field in the BGP message header to ensure it is between 19 and 4096 octets. Reject any message with a Length field outside this range immediately.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP Session Hijacking via OPEN Replay
security_leads.description: Step 1: An attacker captures a valid BGP OPEN message from a legitimate peer. Step 2: The attacker waits for the legitimate BGP session to close. Step 3: The attacker initiates a new TCP connection to the victim BGP speaker and replays the captured OPEN message. Step 4: If the victim BGP speaker does not strictly validate the BGP Identifier or if the attacker can spoof the source IP address, the victim may accept the replayed OPEN message and establish a new BGP session with the attacker. Step 5: The attacker can then send malicious UPDATE messages to hijack traffic. The BGP protocol relies on TCP for connection establishment and does not have built-in mechanisms to prevent replay of the OPEN message across different TCP connections.

rfc_references.quote: After a TCP connection is established, the first message sent by each side is an OPEN message. If the OPEN message is acceptable, a KEEPALIVE message confirming the OPEN is sent back.
If the BGP Identifier field of the OPEN message is syntactically incorrect, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Bad BGP Identifier.

prerequisites: Attacker can capture BGP OPEN messages
Attacker can spoof source IP address or is on-path
TCP MD5 authentication is not enabled
Victim does not strictly validate peer identity beyond BGP Identifier
security_leads.mitigation: Enable TCP MD5 authentication. Use strict peer validation and IPsec for BGP sessions. Implement BGP session monitoring to detect unauthorized session establishments.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker establishes a BGP session with a target router. Step 2: Attacker sends a high volume of UPDATE messages advertising a large number of unique IP prefixes. Step 3: Target router allocates memory for each prefix in its Adj-RIB-In and Loc-RIB. Step 4: Memory exhaustion or CPU overload occurs as the router processes and stores the excessive number of routes, leading to a Denial of Service for legitimate traffic or BGP sessions.

rfc_references.quote: A BGP speaker MAY support the ability to impose a locally-configured, upper bound on the number of address prefixes the speaker is willing to accept from a neighbor. When the upper bound is reached, the speaker, under control of local configuration, either (a) discards new address prefixes from the neighbor... or (b) terminates the BGP connection with the neighbor.

If the UPDATE message contains a feasible route, the Adj-RIB-In will be updated with this route... Otherwise, if the Adj-RIB-In has no route with NLRI identical to the new route, the new route SHALL be placed in the Adj-RIB-In.

prerequisites: Attacker has established a BGP peering session with the target
Target router does not enforce a maximum prefix limit or has a very high limit
security_leads.mitigation: Configure a maximum prefix limit on BGP peers. Implement route filtering using prefix lists or AS-path filters to reject unauthorized or excessive routes. Enable BGP Route Flap Damping.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP UPDATE Message Path Attribute Overflow
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker crafts a BGP UPDATE message with a valid header but sets the Total Path Attribute Length field to a value larger than the actual message payload or the maximum allowed message size (4096 octets). Step 2: The victim BGP speaker parses the Total Path Attribute Length and attempts to allocate a buffer or read data based on this length. Step 3: If the implementation does not strictly validate that the length field does not exceed the remaining message length or the maximum message size, it may read out-of-bounds memory, causing a crash or information leak. Step 4: Alternatively, if the implementation allocates memory based on the length field without checking against system limits, it could lead to resource exhaustion.

rfc_references.quote: Total Path Attribute Length: This 2-octet unsigned integer indicates the total length of the Path Attributes field in octets.

If the Withdrawn Routes Length or Total Attribute Length is too large (i.e., if Withdrawn Routes Length + Total Attribute Length + 23 exceeds the message Length), then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Malformed Attribute List.

prerequisites: Attacker can send BGP UPDATE messages to the victim (e.g., via compromised peer or on-path attack)
Victim implementation fails to validate Total Path Attribute Length against message bounds
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of the Total Path Attribute Length field to ensure it does not exceed the remaining message length or the maximum BGP message size (4096 octets). Use bounds-checked memory allocation and parsing routines.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP UPDATE Message Withdrawn Routes Overflow
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker crafts a BGP UPDATE message with a valid header but sets the Withdrawn Routes Length field to an excessively large value. Step 2: The victim BGP speaker parses the Withdrawn Routes Length and attempts to read the Withdrawn Routes field based on this length. Step 3: If the implementation does not validate that the length field does not exceed the remaining message length, it may read out-of-bounds memory, causing a crash or information leak. Step 4: If the implementation allocates memory based on the length field without checking against system limits, it could lead to resource exhaustion.

rfc_references.quote: Withdrawn Routes Length: This 2-octets unsigned integer indicates the total length of the Withdrawn Routes field in octets.

If the Withdrawn Routes Length or Total Attribute Length is too large (i.e., if Withdrawn Routes Length + Total Attribute Length + 23 exceeds the message Length), then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Malformed Attribute List.

prerequisites: Attacker can send BGP UPDATE messages to the victim
Victim implementation fails to validate Withdrawn Routes Length against message bounds
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of the Withdrawn Routes Length field to ensure it does not exceed the remaining message length or the maximum BGP message size (4096 octets). Use bounds-checked memory allocation and parsing routines.

security_leads.description: Step 1: An on-path attacker intercepts the initial BGP OPEN message from a peer that supports a newer or more secure version of BGP (e.g., BGP-4 with specific capabilities). Step 2: The attacker modifies the 'Version' field in the OPEN message to a lower, supported version (e.g., BGP-3 or an older BGP-4 variant lacking certain security or routing features). Step 3: The receiving peer, following the version negotiation rules, accepts the lower version, resulting in a downgraded session that may lack critical security features, route aggregation capabilities, or modern path attribute handling.

rfc_references.quote: Version: This 1-octet unsigned integer indicates the protocol version number of the message. The current BGP version number is 4.

If the version number in the Version field of the received OPEN message is not supported, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Unsupported Version Number. The Data field is a 2-octet unsigned integer, which indicates the largest, locally-supported version number less than the version the remote BGP peer bid...
BGP speakers MAY negotiate the version of the protocol by making multiple attempts at opening a BGP connection, starting with the highest version number each BGP speaker supports.

prerequisites: attacker is on-path
TCP connection is not protected by TLS or IPsec (BGP uses plain TCP port 179)
both peers support multiple BGP versions
security_leads.mitigation: Implement TCP MD5 authentication (RFC 2385) or BGPsec to protect the BGP session from on-path manipulation. Configure BGP speakers to only accept the highest supported version and reject lower versions explicitly if backward compatibility is not required.

security_leads.description: Step 1: An on-path attacker captures a valid BGP OPEN message and subsequent KEEPALIVE or UPDATE messages during a legitimate BGP session establishment or data exchange. Step 2: The attacker waits for the legitimate session to terminate or for a network disruption to occur. Step 3: The attacker replays the captured OPEN message to the victim BGP speaker to re-establish a session, potentially bypassing authentication if TCP MD5 is not enabled or is misconfigured. Step 4: The attacker replays captured UPDATE messages to inject stale or malicious routing information, causing traffic diversion or blackholing. The protocol lacks built-in sequence numbers or nonces in the BGP message headers to prevent replay of individual messages within a session.

rfc_references.quote: BGP uses TCP [RFC793] as its transport protocol. This eliminates the need to implement explicit update fragmentation, retransmission, acknowledgement, and sequencing.
Because the mechanism defined in the RFC does not provide peer-entity authentication, these connections may be subject to some forms of replay attacks that will not be detected at the TCP layer.
After a TCP connection is established, the first message sent by each side is an OPEN message. If the OPEN message is acceptable, a KEEPALIVE message confirming the OPEN is sent back.

prerequisites: Attacker is on-path or can capture BGP traffic
TCP MD5 authentication is not enabled or is disabled
Attacker can inject packets into the BGP session
security_leads.mitigation: Enable TCP MD5 authentication as specified in RFC 2385 to protect BGP sessions. Use BGPsec for cryptographic validation of route origin and AS path. Implement strict peer validation and monitoring for anomalous session re-establishments.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP Session Impersonation via IP Spoofing
security_leads.description: Step 1: BGP identifies peers primarily by their IP addresses used in the TCP connection and the BGP Identifier in the OPEN message. Step 2: An attacker spoofs the IP address of a legitimate BGP peer. Step 3: The attacker initiates a TCP connection and sends an OPEN message with the legitimate peer's BGP Identifier. If the target router does not strictly validate the source IP against a pre-configured list of authorized peers or relies solely on the TCP connection, the attacker bypasses authentication and establishes a rogue session.

rfc_references.quote: A given BGP speaker sets the value of its BGP Identifier to an IP address that is assigned to that BGP speaker.
There exists a period in which the identity of the peer on the other end of an incoming connection is known, but the BGP identifier is not known.

prerequisites: Attacker can spoof the source IP of a legitimate peer
Target router accepts incoming connections from the spoofed IP
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict ingress/egress filtering (BCP38) to prevent IP spoofing. Configure BGP peers to only accept connections from explicitly authorized IP addresses. Use TCP MD5 to cryptographically bind the session to the authorized peer.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP OPEN Message Collision State Confusion
security_leads.description: Step 1: An attacker establishes a TCP connection to a BGP peer and sends an OPEN message, causing the peer to transition to the OpenConfirm state. Step 2: The attacker simultaneously initiates a second TCP connection to the same peer, creating a connection collision. Step 3: By manipulating the BGP Identifier in the second OPEN message, the attacker forces the peer to evaluate collision resolution logic while in an inconsistent state, potentially causing the peer to drop the legitimate connection or enter an undefined FSM state, leading to a denial of service or session hijacking.

rfc_references.quote: If a pair of BGP speakers try to establish a BGP connection with each other simultaneously, then two parallel connections well be formed... In the event of connection collision, one of the connections MUST be closed.

If a valid OPEN message (BGPOpen (Event 19)) is received, and if the CollisionDetectEstablishedState optional attribute is TRUE, the OPEN message will be checked to see if it collides (Section 6.8) with any other connection.

prerequisites: Attacker can establish TCP connections to the target BGP speaker
Attacker can control the BGP Identifier in the OPEN message
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of BGP Identifiers and enforce collision detection rules consistently across all FSM states. Ensure that connection collision resolution does not leave the FSM in an inconsistent state.

security_leads.description: Step 1: An attacker captures a valid BGP UPDATE message advertising a specific route with certain path attributes. Step 2: The attacker waits for the route to be withdrawn or for network conditions to change. Step 3: The attacker replays the captured UPDATE message to the victim BGP speaker. Step 4: The victim BGP speaker processes the replayed UPDATE message as a new route advertisement, potentially reinstating a withdrawn route or overriding current routing decisions with stale information. The BGP protocol does not include sequence numbers or timestamps in UPDATE messages to ensure freshness.

rfc_references.quote: UPDATE messages are used to transfer routing information between BGP peers. The information in the UPDATE message can be used to construct a graph that describes the relationships of the various Autonomous Systems.

If the UPDATE message contains a feasible route, the Adj-RIB-In will be updated with this route as follows: if the NLRI of the new route is identical to the one the route currently has stored in the Adj-RIB-In, then the new route SHALL replace the older route in the Adj-RIB-In, thus implicitly withdrawing the older route from service.

prerequisites: Attacker can capture BGP UPDATE messages
Attacker can inject packets into the BGP session
TCP MD5 authentication is not enabled
security_leads.mitigation: Enable TCP MD5 authentication. Use BGPsec to ensure route freshness and validity. Implement route monitoring and anomaly detection systems to identify unexpected route reinstatements.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP Identifier Internal IP Address Leakage
security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker establishes a TCP connection with a peer. Step 2: The speaker sends an OPEN message containing the 'BGP Identifier' field. Step 3: The protocol specifies that the BGP Identifier is set to an IP address assigned to the BGP speaker. Step 4: If the BGP speaker uses an internal/private IP address (e.g., from RFC 1918 space) as its BGP Identifier, this internal network topology information is leaked to the peer, potentially aiding an attacker in mapping the internal network structure.

rfc_references.quote: BGP Identifier: This 4-octet unsigned integer indicates the BGP Identifier of the sender. A given BGP speaker sets the value of its BGP Identifier to an IP address that is assigned to that BGP speaker.

prerequisites: Attacker is a legitimate BGP peer or can spoof a BGP peer
BGP speaker is configured to use an internal/private IP address as its BGP Identifier
security_leads.mitigation: Configure the BGP speaker to use a publicly routable IP address or a dedicated loopback address that does not reveal internal subnetting details as the BGP Identifier.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP Session Teardown via Malformed Messages
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker establishes a BGP session with a target router. Step 2: Attacker sends a BGP message (e.g., UPDATE or OPEN) with intentionally malformed fields (e.g., invalid length, unrecognized attribute flags, or syntactically incorrect NLRI). Step 3: Target router detects the error and sends a NOTIFICATION message. Step 4: Target router closes the BGP connection and clears associated Adj-RIB-In entries, causing a temporary loss of routing information and potential traffic disruption.

rfc_references.quote: When any of the conditions described here are detected, a NOTIFICATION message... is sent, and the BGP connection is closed... the associated Adj-RIB-In has been cleared, and all resources for that BGP connection have been deallocated.
All errors detected while processing the UPDATE message MUST be indicated by sending the NOTIFICATION message with the Error Code UPDATE Message Error.

prerequisites: Attacker has established a BGP peering session with the target
Attacker can craft and send BGP messages
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict input validation on BGP message parsers. Use BGP Graceful Restart to maintain forwarding state during session resets. Monitor for frequent BGP session resets and alert administrators.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker establishes a BGP session with a target router. Step 2: Attacker sends UPDATE messages with excessively large Path Attributes or NLRI fields, approaching the maximum BGP message size of 4096 bytes. Step 3: Target router allocates memory and CPU resources to parse and process these large messages. Step 4: Repeated sending of large messages can exhaust memory or CPU resources, leading to a Denial of Service.

rfc_references.quote: if the Length field of the message header is less than 19 or greater than 4096... then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Bad Message Length.
An UPDATE message is used to advertise feasible routes that share common path attributes to a peer, or to withdraw multiple unfeasible routes from service.

prerequisites: Attacker has established a BGP peering session with the target
Attacker can craft BGP messages with large payloads
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict limits on the size of BGP messages and path attributes. Use route filtering to reject routes with excessive path attributes. Monitor for unusually large BGP messages.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP OPEN Message Optional Parameters Overflow
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker crafts a BGP OPEN message with a valid header but sets the Opt Parm Len field to a value larger than the actual optional parameters data or the maximum allowed message size. Step 2: The victim BGP speaker parses the Opt Parm Len and attempts to read the Optional Parameters field based on this length. Step 3: If the implementation does not validate that the length field does not exceed the remaining message length, it may read out-of-bounds memory, causing a crash or information leak. Step 4: If the implementation allocates memory based on the length field without checking against system limits, it could lead to resource exhaustion.

rfc_references.quote: Optional Parameters Length: This 1-octet unsigned integer indicates the total length of the Optional Parameters field in octets.
If one of the Optional Parameters in the OPEN message is recognized, but is malformed, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to 0 (Unspecific).

prerequisites: Attacker can send BGP OPEN messages to the victim
Victim implementation fails to validate Opt Parm Len against message bounds
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of the Opt Parm Len field to ensure it does not exceed the remaining message length or the maximum BGP message size (4096 octets). Use bounds-checked memory allocation and parsing routines.

security_leads.technique_name: Ambiguous NEXT_HOP Resolution in EBGP Multihop
security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker sends an UPDATE to an external peer multiple IP hops away. Step 2: The RFC states the speaker 'MAY be configured to propagate the NEXT_HOP attribute' or 'By default, the BGP speaker SHOULD use the IP address of the interface...'. Step 3: Different implementations may default to propagating the original NEXT_HOP or changing it to the local interface, leading to asymmetric routing or blackholing if the receiving peer cannot resolve the propagated NEXT_HOP.

rfc_references.quote: When sending a message to an external peer X, and the peer is multiple IP hops away from the speaker... The speaker MAY be configured to propagate the NEXT_HOP attribute... By default, the BGP speaker SHOULD use the IP address of the interface that the speaker uses in the NEXT_HOP attribute to establish the BGP connection to peer X.

prerequisites: EBGP multihop session
Misaligned NEXT_HOP configuration between peers
security_leads.mitigation: Explicitly configure NEXT_HOP behavior on multihop EBGP sessions to ensure both peers agree on whether the NEXT_HOP is preserved or rewritten.

security_leads.description: Step 1: An on-path attacker intercepts the BGP OPEN message containing the 'Optional Parameters' field, which carries capabilities (e.g., Route Refresh, Multiprotocol Extensions). Step 2: The attacker strips or modifies the Optional Parameters to remove specific capability advertisements, effectively downgrading the negotiated feature set. Step 3: The receiving peer processes the OPEN message without the advertised capabilities, leading to a session that lacks advanced routing features or security extensions, potentially causing suboptimal routing or reduced resilience.

rfc_references.quote: Optional Parameters: This field contains a list of optional parameters, in which each parameter is encoded as a <Parameter Type, Parameter Length, Parameter Value> triplet. [RFC3392] defines the Capabilities Optional Parameter.
If one of the Optional Parameters in the OPEN message is not recognized, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Unsupported Optional Parameters.

prerequisites: attacker is on-path
TCP connection lacks integrity protection
peer relies on optional capabilities for optimal operation
security_leads.mitigation: Use TCP MD5 (RFC 2385) or BGPsec to ensure the integrity of the OPEN message and its optional parameters. Validate and strictly enforce required capabilities during the BGP session establishment.

security_leads.description: Step 1: The BGP OPEN message contains the 'My Autonomous System' and 'BGP Identifier' fields which are used for peer identification. Step 2: The RFC states that the determination of acceptable Autonomous System numbers is outside the scope of the protocol. Step 3: An attacker can craft an OPEN message with arbitrary AS numbers or BGP Identifiers. If the receiving router does not enforce strict policy validation on these fields, the attacker can bypass logical authentication checks and establish a session under a false identity.

rfc_references.quote: If the Autonomous System field of the OPEN message is unacceptable, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Bad Peer AS. The determination of acceptable Autonomous System numbers is outside the scope of this protocol.
My Autonomous System: This 2-octet unsigned integer indicates the Autonomous System number of the sender.

prerequisites: Attacker has established a TCP connection to the BGP speaker
Target router does not enforce strict AS number or BGP Identifier validation policies
security_leads.mitigation: Configure BGP speakers to strictly validate the 'My Autonomous System' and 'BGP Identifier' fields in the OPEN message against pre-configured expected values for each peer. Reject OPEN messages that do not match the expected peer identity.

security_leads.technique_name: Inconsistent Handling of Unrecognized Optional Transitive Attributes
security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker receives an UPDATE with an unrecognized optional transitive attribute. Step 2: The RFC states the path 'SHOULD be accepted' and the attribute 'MUST be passed... with the Partial bit... set to 1'. Step 3: Implementations may differ in how they handle the 'SHOULD' (some may reject), and variations in Partial bit handling can cause route oscillation or incorrect path selection in downstream peers that interpret the Partial bit differently.

rfc_references.quote: Paths with unrecognized transitive optional attributes SHOULD be accepted. If a path with an unrecognized transitive optional attribute is accepted and passed to other BGP peers, then the unrecognized transitive optional attribute of that path MUST be passed, along with the path, to other BGP peers with the Partial bit in the Attribute Flags octet set to 1.

prerequisites: Presence of non-standard or extension BGP attributes
Heterogeneous BGP implementations in the path
security_leads.mitigation: Ensure all BGP speakers in a domain support the same set of optional attributes, or configure strict filtering to drop unrecognized optional transitive attributes if interoperability is an issue.

security_leads.technique_name: BGP AS_PATH Attribute Segment Length Overflow
security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker crafts a BGP UPDATE message with a valid AS_PATH attribute but sets the path segment length field to an excessively large value. Step 2: The victim BGP speaker parses the path segment length and attempts to read the path segment value based on this length. Step 3: If the implementation does not validate that the length field does not exceed the remaining attribute length or message length, it may read out-of-bounds memory, causing a crash or information leak. Step 4: If the implementation allocates memory based on the length field without checking against system limits, it could lead to resource exhaustion.

rfc_references.quote: The path segment length is a 1-octet length field, containing the number of ASes (not the number of octets) in the path segment value field.
The AS_PATH attribute is checked for syntactic correctness. If the path is syntactically incorrect, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Malformed AS_PATH.

prerequisites: Attacker can send BGP UPDATE messages to the victim
Victim implementation fails to validate AS_PATH segment length against attribute/message bounds
security_leads.mitigation: Implement strict validation of the AS_PATH segment length field to ensure it does not exceed the remaining attribute length or message length. Use bounds-checked memory allocation and parsing routines.

security_leads.description: Step 1: BGP uses a collision resolution mechanism based on BGP Identifiers when two peers try to establish a connection simultaneously. Step 2: An attacker monitors BGP traffic or initiates a connection at the same time as a legitimate peer. Step 3: By manipulating the timing or the BGP Identifier in the OPEN message, the attacker can influence the collision resolution process to force the closure of the legitimate peer's connection and establish their own, bypassing the intended peer relationship.

rfc_references.quote: Based on the value of the BGP Identifier, a convention is established for detecting which BGP connection is to be preserved when a collision occurs. The convention is to compare the BGP Identifiers of the peers involved in the collision and to retain only the connection initiated by the BGP speaker with the higher-valued BGP Identifier.
This is referred to as a connection collision (see Section 6.8).

prerequisites: Attacker can initiate TCP connections to the target BGP speaker
Attacker can predict or influence the timing of the legitimate peer's connection attempts
security_leads.mitigation: Use TCP MD5 authentication to prevent unauthorized peers from establishing TCP connections. Implement strict peer validation to ensure that only authorized BGP Identifiers are accepted, regardless of collision resolution outcomes.

security_leads.technique_name: UPDATE Message Path Attribute Parsing State Confusion
security_leads.description: Step 1: An attacker sends an UPDATE message with malformed or out-of-order path attributes. Step 2: The BGP speaker's parser enters an error state while processing the attributes, but the FSM remains in the Established state. Step 3: Subsequent valid UPDATE messages are processed incorrectly due to the lingering parser state, causing the BGP speaker to install incorrect routes or drop valid updates, leading to routing instability or traffic hijacking.

rfc_references.quote: The sender of an UPDATE message SHOULD order path attributes within the UPDATE message in ascending order of attribute type. The receiver of an UPDATE message MUST be prepared to handle path attributes within UPDATE messages that are out of order.
If any recognized attribute has Attribute Flags that conflict with the Attribute Type Code, then the Error Subcode MUST be set to Attribute Flags Error.

prerequisites: Attacker can send UPDATE messages to the target BGP speaker
Target BGP speaker has a parser that does not fully reset state on attribute errors
security_leads.mitigation: Ensure that the BGP parser fully resets its state after processing each UPDATE message, regardless of errors. Implement strict validation of path attribute order and flags.

security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker receives an UPDATE message from a peer. Step 2: The UPDATE message contains the AS_PATH attribute, which lists the Autonomous Systems the route has traversed. Step 3: This information reveals the inter-AS connectivity graph and routing policies (e.g., transit vs. stub relationships) to any observer on the BGP session. Step 4: An attacker can use this information to map the internet topology, identify critical transit providers, and plan more targeted routing attacks (e.g., BGP hijacking or route poisoning).

rfc_references.quote: AS_PATH (Type Code 2): AS_PATH is a well-known mandatory attribute that is composed of a sequence of AS path segments... The path segment value field contains one or more AS numbers...

This network reachability information includes information on the list of Autonomous Systems (ASes) that reachability information traverses. This information is sufficient for constructing a graph of AS connectivity...

prerequisites: Attacker has access to BGP UPDATE messages (e.g., via a peer session or on-path sniffing)
security_leads.mitigation: Use BGP route filtering and prefix lists to limit the amount of routing information shared with untrusted peers. Consider using BGP communities or other policy mechanisms to obscure specific routing policies if necessary, though this is inherently difficult in a path-vector protocol.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker establishes a BGP session with a target router. Step 2: Attacker stops sending KEEPALIVE or UPDATE messages. Step 3: Target router's Hold Timer expires. Step 4: Target router sends a NOTIFICATION message and closes the BGP connection, leading to a loss of routing information for that peer.

rfc_references.quote: If a system does not receive successive KEEPALIVE, UPDATE, and/or NOTIFICATION messages within the period specified in the Hold Time field of the OPEN message, then the NOTIFICATION message with the Hold Timer Expired Error Code is sent and the BGP connection is closed.
The Hold Time MUST be either zero or at least three seconds.

prerequisites: Attacker has established a BGP peering session with the target
Attacker can control the sending of BGP messages
security_leads.mitigation: Configure appropriate Hold Timer values. Implement BGP Graceful Restart to maintain forwarding state during session resets. Monitor for unexpected BGP session teardowns.

security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker advertises a route in an UPDATE message. Step 2: The UPDATE message includes the NEXT_HOP attribute, which specifies the IP address of the next hop router. Step 3: If the NEXT_HOP address is an internal IP address (e.g., in an iBGP session or due to misconfiguration in eBGP), it reveals internal network addressing to the peer. Step 4: This information can be used by an attacker to map internal network segments and identify critical infrastructure.

rfc_references.quote: NEXT_HOP (Type Code 3): This is a well-known mandatory attribute that defines the (unicast) IP address of the router that SHOULD be used as the next hop to the destinations listed in the Network Layer Reachability Information field of the UPDATE message.

prerequisites: Attacker is a BGP peer
BGP speaker advertises routes with internal NEXT_HOP addresses to external peers
security_leads.mitigation: Ensure that eBGP sessions advertise routes with the next-hop address set to the local BGP speaker's IP address (as per standard eBGP behavior) and that iBGP sessions are restricted to internal peers only.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Attacker initiates multiple simultaneous BGP connection attempts to a target router. Step 2: Target router processes connection collision detection logic. Step 3: Attacker manipulates BGP Identifiers to force the target to repeatedly close and reopen connections. Step 4: Excessive connection churn consumes CPU and memory resources on the target router, potentially leading to a Denial of Service.

rfc_references.quote: If a pair of BGP speakers try to establish a BGP connection with each other simultaneously, then two parallel connections well be formed... In the event of connection collision, one of the connections MUST be closed.
If a connection in the OpenSent state is determined to be the connection that must be closed, an OpenCollisionDump (Event 23) is signaled to the state machine.

prerequisites: Attacker can initiate TCP connections to the target router on port 179
Attacker can control BGP Identifiers in OPEN messages
security_leads.mitigation: Implement rate limiting on incoming BGP connection attempts. Use TCP MD5 authentication to prevent unauthorized connection attempts. Monitor for excessive BGP connection churn.

security_leads.description: Step 1: A BGP speaker prepends its AS to an AS_SEQUENCE that is already at the 255 AS limit. Step 2: The RFC states it 'SHOULD prepend a new segment of type AS_SEQUENCE'. Step 3: Implementations may differ in whether they strictly enforce the 255 limit per segment, how they handle the new segment creation, or whether they drop the route, leading to inconsistent AS_PATH lengths and potential route rejection by strict peers.

rfc_references.quote: if the first path segment of the AS_PATH is of type AS_SEQUENCE, the local system prepends its own AS number as the last element of the sequence... If the act of prepending will cause an overflow in the AS_PATH segment (i.e., more than 255 ASes), it SHOULD prepend a new segment of type AS_SEQUENCE and prepend its own AS number to this new segment.

prerequisites: Route with AS_PATH near 255 AS limit
AS_PATH prepending configured
security_leads.mitigation: Monitor AS_PATH lengths and avoid excessive prepending. Ensure implementations correctly handle AS_PATH segment overflow by creating new segments as specified.

security_leads.description: Step 1: Two BGP speakers simultaneously initiate connections to each other. Step 2: The RFC specifies collision resolution based on BGP Identifier comparison. Step 3: The RFC states 'A BGP speaker MAY also examine connections in an OpenSent state if it knows the BGP Identifier of the peer by means outside of the protocol.' Implementations that do not examine OpenSent connections may temporarily maintain duplicate sessions or resolve collisions differently, causing brief routing instability.

rfc_references.quote: Upon receipt of an OPEN message, the local system MUST examine all of its connections that are in the OpenConfirm state. A BGP speaker MAY also examine connections in an OpenSent state if it knows the BGP Identifier of the peer by means outside of the protocol.

prerequisites: Simultaneous BGP connection attempts
Heterogeneous BGP implementations
security_leads.mitigation: Configure BGP sessions to initiate connections sequentially or use passive/active roles to avoid simultaneous connection attempts.

security_leads.description: Step 1: An attacker sends a KEEPALIVE message with a manipulated Hold Time value during the OPEN message exchange. Step 2: The BGP speaker accepts the manipulated Hold Time and transitions to the OpenConfirm state. Step 3: The attacker stops sending KEEPALIVE messages, causing the Hold Timer to expire prematurely. The BGP speaker transitions to the Idle state, dropping the connection and potentially causing routing flaps.

rfc_references.quote: Upon receipt of an OPEN message, a BGP speaker MUST calculate the value of the Hold Timer by using the smaller of its configured Hold Time and the Hold Time received in the OPEN message.

If a system does not receive successive KEEPALIVE, UPDATE, and/or NOTIFICATION messages within the period specified in the Hold Time field of the OPEN message, then the NOTIFICATION message with the Hold Timer Expired Error Code is sent and the BGP connection is closed.

prerequisites: Attacker can send OPEN messages to the target BGP speaker
Target BGP speaker does not enforce a minimum Hold Time
security_leads.mitigation: Enforce a minimum Hold Time value and validate the Hold Time field in OPEN messages. Ensure that the Hold Timer is not manipulated by malicious peers.
